conversation.content: Design a social media news feed. Think about it from the user's perspective first. What makes a great feed experience?

A great feed experience is one that keeps users informed and engaged without feeling overwhelming or manipulative. The feed should surface content that's relevant to the user, balance recency with importance, and feel personalized. Key dimensions: relevance — showing content from people and topics you care about. Diversity — not just showing the same type of content repeatedly. Freshness — a feed that feels alive and updating. And control — letting users customize what they see.
Great product intuition. Now, how do you measure feed quality? What metrics tell you the feed is working well?

I'd look at both engagement and satisfaction metrics. Engagement: time spent in feed, scroll depth, interaction rate — likes, comments, shares, and clicks per session. Satisfaction: we can use periodic surveys — net promoter score for the feed — and implicit signals like session frequency. A tricky metric is 'meaningful social interactions' — are users engaging with friends or just consuming viral content? We should track close-friend interaction rate separately. Counter-metrics to watch: unfollow rate, mute rate, and 'time well spent' scores. If engagement goes up but users report feeling worse, we have a problem.
How do you balance engagement optimization with user well-being? This is a real tension.

It is a real tension. Pure engagement optimization tends to promote outrage and sensationalism because those drive clicks. My approach: define a multi-objective ranking function. Instead of maximizing P(click), we optimize a weighted combination: 0.4 * P(meaningful_interaction) + 0.3 * P(value_to_user) + 0.2 * P(engagement) + 0.1 * P(content_diversity). 'Value to user' is predicted from survey responses — we periodically ask 'was this post worth seeing?' and train a model on those labels. We also apply hard constraints: demote content that triggers the integrity classifier, cap the proportion of reshared vs original content, and enforce a minimum diversity score per feed page.
How would you set up the A/B testing framework to validate changes to the ranking model?

The A/B framework needs to handle several challenges. First, user-level randomization — hash the user ID to assign them to control or treatment to avoid network effects within a user's sessions. Second, we need holdback groups: 5% of users always get the previous ranking model as a long-term baseline. Third, experiment sizing: with 500M DAU, even a 1% experiment gives us 5M users, enough to detect 0.1% changes in engagement. Fourth, the metric suite: we track primary metrics (session time, meaningful interactions), secondary metrics (all engagement signals), and guardrail metrics (unfollow rate, report rate, regretful engagement). An experiment passes only if primary metrics improve AND guardrail metrics don't degrade. Typical experiment duration is 2 weeks to account for novelty effects.
Good framework. Now let's get into the system architecture. How does the feed get generated?

The feed generation pipeline has four stages. Stage 1 — candidate sourcing: pull the latest 1000 posts from people you follow, groups you're in, and pages you've liked. Also inject 100-200 candidates from recommendation models — content from accounts you don't follow but might like. Stage 2 — pre-filtering: remove posts you've already seen, posts from muted accounts, posts flagged by integrity systems. Down to maybe 500 candidates. Stage 3 — scoring: the ranking model scores each candidate. It's a deep learning model with features like user-post affinity, post quality score, recency, social proof signals. Stage 4 — post-processing: apply diversity rules, inject ads at specified positions, apply any experiment treatments. Output: an ordered feed of 50 posts for the first page.
That ranking model — how do you keep it fresh? User interests change, content evolves.

Model freshness happens at two timescales. The model itself is retrained daily on the last 7 days of engagement data. Training happens on a GPU cluster overnight, and the new model is A/B tested against the current production model before full rollout — automated model validation. But daily retraining doesn't capture real-time trends. So we also use real-time features: the post's engagement velocity in the last hour, the user's recent activity in this session, and trending topic signals. These features are computed by a streaming pipeline and injected at serving time. The model weights are static, but the features are live. This gives us the responsiveness of real-time without the instability of continuous model updates.
How do you handle the 'filter bubble' problem? If the ranking model optimizes for engagement, users only see reinforcing content.

Filter bubbles are a real risk. I'd address this at multiple levels. In the candidate sourcing stage, we explicitly include a 'serendipity' allocation — 10-15% of candidates come from outside the user's typical interest graph. These are selected using an explore-exploit framework: Thompson sampling to balance showing content the user will likely enjoy vs content that broadens their exposure. In the ranking stage, we add a diversity penalty: after selecting the top-ranked post, we discount subsequent posts that are too similar in topic or source. This is a maximum marginal relevance approach. We also track a per-user diversity score over time and boost diverse content for users whose consumption is becoming too narrow.
Let's discuss the infrastructure. How do you serve feeds at 500M DAU scale?

At 500M DAU, with users checking feeds maybe 10 times a day, that's 5 billion feed requests per day, or about 58,000 QPS average with peaks at 3-4x, so 200K QPS at peak. The feed serving stack: a CDN layer for static assets like images and videos embedded in posts. Behind it, a feed service that orchestrates the pipeline I described. The ranking model runs on a GPU inference fleet for the heavy neural network scoring, or we use distilled CPU-friendly models if latency is a concern. The candidate sourcing queries a social graph service and a post store — both heavily cached. I'd pre-compute feed candidates for active users during off-peak hours and cache them, then apply real-time re-ranking at request time. This amortizes the expensive candidate sourcing.
A breaking news event happens — say an earthquake. Millions of users post about it simultaneously. How does the feed handle this?

Breaking news creates two problems: write amplification from millions of new posts, and read amplification as users flood the app. For writes, the post ingestion pipeline needs to handle the spike — Kafka absorbs the burst, and downstream consumers auto-scale. For the feed, the breaking news posts will naturally rank high due to recency and engagement velocity. But we should also detect the event explicitly: when a topic's volume exceeds 10x its baseline in a 10-minute window, we trigger a 'breaking event' mode. In this mode, we inject a dedicated breaking news module at the top of the feed that's curated from high-credibility sources. We also temporarily boost chronological ordering for event-related content so users get the latest updates. After the event subsides, we gradually return to normal ranking.
How do you handle misinformation during such an event? False information spreads fastest in the first few hours.

Misinformation during breaking events is one of the hardest problems. Immediate measures: reduce the ranking boost for reshared content during breaking events — original reporting should be prioritized over viral reshares. Apply a 'distribution friction' to posts that are spreading unusually fast but haven't been verified — not removing them, but slowing their spread by reducing their ranking score by 50%. Surface authoritative sources: partner with fact-checking organizations and news agencies, boost their content. Longer-term: an ML model trained on known misinformation patterns — sensational language, manipulated images, accounts with low credibility scores. Label flagged content with a context banner. And critically, provide users with tools to see multiple perspectives on the same event.
How do you handle the feed for users who follow thousands of accounts? Their candidate set is massive.

For heavy users following 5,000+ accounts, sourcing candidates from all of them is expensive. I'd use a tiered approach. Tier 1: close friends and high-affinity accounts — always fetch their recent posts. We identify these from interaction frequency. Maybe the top 50 accounts. Tier 2: accounts the user interacts with occasionally — sample their recent posts, maybe the top 200. Tier 3: the remaining thousands — use a lightweight model to predict which are most likely to have relevant content now, and only fetch from those. This reduces the candidate sourcing from O(5000) to O(300) while preserving feed quality. We validate this with an A/B test measuring 'post from followed account not shown that would have been engaged with' as a miss metric.
Final question: if you were launching this feed from scratch, what would you build in the first version and what would you defer?

V1: reverse-chronological feed from followed accounts. Simple, transparent, easy to debug. Pre-compute timelines using fan-out on write for all users. Basic ranking by recency only. A simple A/B framework to start collecting engagement data. Phase 2: introduce a lightweight ranking model using features like recency, author-user affinity, and post engagement count. Phase 3: the full ML ranking pipeline with diversity, well-being constraints, and the multi-stage architecture. I'd defer: recommendation of content from non-followed accounts, advanced trending detection, and the breaking news module. You need to get the core feed right before adding complexity.
Great product and system thinking. Thanks for the discussion.

strengths: Exceptional product thinking — multi-objective ranking with well-being constraints
Strong A/B testing framework with guardrail metrics and automated validation
Thoughtful approach to filter bubbles using explore-exploit and diversity penalties
weaknesses: Capacity estimation was thin — didn't calculate storage, bandwidth, or infrastructure costs
API design was not discussed — no endpoint contracts or data models
Database choices and data modeling were not explored in depth
